case_brief.incident_description: Naledi had worked for the agency for three years. She told her manager that she was pregnant and two weeks later was informed that her role was redundant. She says the business had recently won two new clients, that another junior employee in the same team was retained, and that she received no written section 189(3) notice or meaningful consultation before the decision. letter:
Background

1. We are instructed by Ms Naledi Dlamini in connection with the termination of her employment with Orbit Creative Agency (Pty) Ltd. This letter is written without prejudice and subject to contract, is not to be construed as an admission of any fact or liability on the part of our client, and is sent on the basis that all of our client's rights are reserved to proceed to the appropriate forum without further notice should a satisfactory resolution not be reached.

2. Our client was employed by Orbit Creative Agency for a period she describes as approximately three years, in a junior role within a team structure. We are instructed to proceed on this account of her service pending confirmation of the precise commencement date and any documentary record held by the Employer.

3. On a date in October 2026, our client disclosed to her manager that she was pregnant. Approximately two weeks later, she was informed that her role was being made redundant. The Employer has characterised the decision as a restructuring exercise. We note that the retrenchment concerned our client alone within her team rather than a wider group, and the process owed to her is accordingly assessed against the standard consultation requirements of section 189 of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995.

4. Our client's instructions are that the agency had recently secured two new clients in the period immediately preceding her dismissal, a fact which, if confirmed, sits uneasily with a genuine operational need to reduce headcount in her team. Our client further instructs that a junior colleague performing a materially similar role within the same team was retained, and that she alone was identified for retrenchment.

5. Our client instructs that she received no written notice in terms of section 189(3) of the LRA setting out the reasons for the proposed retrenchment, the alternatives considered, the proposed selection criteria or the severance proposed, and that no meaningful consultation process took place before the decision was communicated to her as final. She was offered one month's notice and severance pay.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: operational requirements under section 188(1) read with the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025: Any dismissal must be for a fair reason and effected in accordance with a fair procedure under section 188(1) of the LRA. Where an employer relies on operational requirements, the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, at paragraphs 22 to 24, read with section 189 of the LRA, requires that the operational rationale be genuine, that consultation be meaningful and that selection criteria be objective and fairly applied. On our client's instructions, no section 189(3) notice was issued and no consultation process of any kind took place before the decision was presented to her as final. The absence of any opportunity to engage on the rationale, the alternatives or the selection criteria is, on its own, a significant procedural defect. To the extent that the Employer's recent acquisition of two new clients is confirmed, it raises a real question as to whether a genuine operational need existed at all. The retention of another junior employee performing similar work in the same team, if confirmed, further calls into question whether any selection criteria applied were objective or fairly applied as between our client and her colleague.

2. Automatically unfair dismissal linked to pregnancy under section 187(1)(e) of the LRA: A dismissal is automatically unfair where the reason for the dismissal is the employee's pregnancy or any reason related to pregnancy, in terms of section 187(1)(e) of the LRA. Our client disclosed her pregnancy to her manager and was informed approximately two weeks later that her position was redundant. That sequence, considered together with the absence of any section 189(3) notice, the absence of meaningful consultation, the timing relative to the acquisition of two new clients and the retention of a comparator employee in a similar role, raises a material question as to the true reason for the dismissal. Where a dismissal is found to be automatically unfair, the compensation ceiling under section 194(3) of the LRA extends to 24 months' remuneration, materially beyond the 12-month ceiling that applies to an ordinary unfair dismissal under section 194(1). This higher ceiling is directly relevant to the settlement calibration proposed below.

3. Statutory entitlements on termination: confirmation required: Independently of the fairness of the dismissal, our client's entitlement to notice, or payment in lieu of notice, is governed by section 37 of the BCEA, which determines the applicable notice period, read with section 38 of the BCEA, which creates the entitlement to payment instead of notice, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement. We are instructed that one month's notice and a severance payment were offered. We require confirmation that the notice period and the severance calculation correctly reflect the entitlements created by sections 37, 38 and 41 of the BCEA respectively, by reference to our client's completed years of service; the mechanics of each entitlement are addressed in the settlement terms below.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without conceding any of the above and on a without prejudice and subject to contract basis, our client is amenable to resolving this matter on a sensible commercial footing at this stage, in preference to referral to the CCMA. We record that the window for referral under section 191(1)(b)(i) of the LRA remains open. Our client proposes the following terms of settlement:

• Compensation on an ex gratia, total cost to company basis. In light of the cumulative procedural defects identified above, together with the disputed substantive basis for dismissal and the safety context giving rise to the allegation, our client's position is that settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, being up to twelve months' remuneration

• Payment in lieu of notice calculated by reference to the applicable notice period under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, with payment made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA

• Confirmation and payment of accrued and untaken leave pay owed under section 40 of the BCEA

• Confirmation that severance pay has been correctly calculated and paid in terms of section 41 of the BCEA, by reference to our client's completed years of service

• Confirmation that provident or pension fund contributions, where applicable, are paid up to date and that the accumulated benefit will be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the fund

• Confirmation that UIF contributions are paid up to date and delivery of a completed UI-19 certificate

• A certificate of service in terms of section 42 of the BCEA

• An agreed positive or neutral reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties

• A written undertaking by the Employer and its representatives not to disparage our client, whether to prospective employers or otherwise

• Confidentiality as to the terms of settlement, the negotiations and the existence of this dispute as between the parties and their respective advisers

• The settlement to be recorded in a formal written settlement agreement signed by both parties, with all of our client's rights reserved until such agreement is concluded

Our client's claims, taken together, disclose both a materially defective retrenchment process and a credible question as to whether pregnancy was a material reason for the termination. These are matters that a commissioner at the CCMA would be entitled to scrutinise closely, including by reference to the timing of events, the absence of any section 189(3) notice, the absence of consultation, the treatment of the comparator employee and the Employer's trading position at the relevant time. Resolution at this stage avoids the cost, delay and uncertainty of referral proceedings for both parties.

We invite a substantive response within seven calendar days of the date of this letter, failing which our client's instructions are to proceed to refer this matter to the CCMA without further notice. All of our client's rights in this regard are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: The settlement terms paragraph introduces an unsupported fact not in the case brief: a reference to 'the safety context giving rise to the allegation'. There is no safety or OHSA issue anywhere in the brief; this is an invented fact bleeding in from an unrelated template. This is a material fidelity breach even though other facts (pregnancy, timing, comparator, two new clients, no s189(3) notice, no consultation, one month notice and severance) are all accurately drawn from the brief and appropriately hedged with 'our client instructs' / 'to the extent confirmed'.
criteria.required_fix: Remove the reference to a 'safety context' entirely; it has no basis in the brief. Recalibrate the sentence to refer only to the procedural defects (no s189(3) notice, no consultation) and the pregnancy-linked timing actually supported by the facts.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "together with the disputed substantive basis for dismissal and the safety context giving rise to the allegation, our client's position is that settlement should be calibrated..."

criteria.problem: The matter is HIGH merit (substantive 9, procedural 10) with AUD override (pregnancy) carrying a 24-month cap under s194(3), yet the settlement compensation clause anchors calibration only to the ordinary 12-month cap under section 194(1) despite the body text correctly identifying the 24-month AUD ceiling as 'directly relevant to the settlement calibration'. This is an internal inconsistency: the legal analysis flags the higher ceiling but the operative settlement term reverts to the lower cap, undercutting the leverage the brief supports. This is also the 'too generic compensation' defect under the mandatory HIGH-merit check: the clause gestures at 'cumulative procedural defects' and 'disputed substantive basis' but does not concretely tie the proposed level to the specific override triggers (pregnancy timing, absence of s189(3) notice, absence of consultation, comparator retention, implausible operational rationale).
criteria.required_fix: Align the settlement compensation clause with the 24-month s194(3) AUD ceiling given the pregnancy-linked override, and explicitly connect the proposed settlement level to the specific confirmed risk factors: no s189(3) notice, no consultation, comparator retention, timing relative to pregnancy disclosure and the new-client acquisitions.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "our client's position is that settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, being up to twelve months' remuneration" versus body text: "the compensation ceiling under section 194(3) of the LRA extends to 24 months' remuneration... This higher ceiling is directly relevant to the settlement calibration proposed below."

criteria.problem: Tone is professional, measured, proportionate and consistent with the counterparty-facing profile; hedging language ('to the extent confirmed', 'if confirmed', 'our client instructs') is used appropriately throughout. Minor stylistic lapse: the phrase 'commercial footing' and general register are fine, but the invented safety reference also damages tone credibility since it is a non-sequitur a respondent's lawyer would notice.
criteria.required_fix: Remove the stray safety reference so the tone reads as consistently controlled and evidence-based throughout.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "We are instructed by Ms Naledi Dlamini..."; "To the extent that the Employer's recent acquisition of two new clients is confirmed..."

criteria.problem: Overall structure is logical: background then legal claims then settlement then conclusion, consistent with the standing body order. However, the standing order at 3A.1 calls for a single consolidated settlement preamble and clause set with no earlier duplication, which is observed here, but the legal claims section merges retrenchment substantive and procedural fairness into one claim and compensation framing is split across two places (legal claim text and settlement clause), creating slight redundancy and a small structural seam where the 24-month cap is raised then abandoned.
criteria.required_fix: Ensure the legal-claims-to-settlement progression is internally consistent, particularly on the compensation cap carried through to the settlement clause.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Claim 2 raises the 24-month cap; settlement term 1 reverts to 12 months, creating a jarring progression.

The notice-pay clause itself is correctly framed as complementary (section 37 period, section 38 payment mechanism), which is compliant.
criteria.required_fix: Recalibrate the headline compensation clause to the 24-month AUD-linked ceiling with an explicit tie to the specific risk factors, keep the response window at seven days (already compliant).
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, being up to twelve months' remuneration" despite the s194(3) 24-month ceiling being flagged as applicable.

forensic_questions: What is the exact date of the pregnancy disclosure to the manager, and is there any written record (email, WhatsApp, HR system note) of that disclosure and the date?

Is there any documentary evidence (press release, client contract, internal announcement) confirming the timing of the two new client wins relative to the dismissal?
Did Ms Dlamini receive anything in writing describing the decision as 'restructuring', and if so can a copy be provided?

criteria.problem: The first settlement term inserts an invented fact not present anywhere in the case brief: it references 'the safety context giving rise to the allegation' as a basis for calibrating settlement. There is no safety issue, allegation, or OHSA-type fact in this matter at all; this is a fabricated element, likely carried over from a different template or matter, and it is a serious factual contamination. Separately, the retrenchment headcount in the brief is 'Just me' (a single-employee retrenchment) and this is never stated or used to inform forum/track framing, which is a completeness gap rather than invention.
criteria.required_fix: Delete the phrase referencing 'the safety context giving rise to the allegation' entirely; it has no basis in the brief. Recalibrate the settlement rationale to rely only on confirmed/conditional facts: pregnancy timing, absence of s189(3) notice, absence of consultation, comparator retention and questionable operational rationale.

This is an internal inconsistency between the AUD claim (24 months) and the settlement calibration (expressly capped at 12 months), and compounded by the extraneous 'safety context' insertion which further muddies the stated rationale.

As currently drafted the settlement undersells a HIGH merit matter.

Pregnancy-AUD claim is properly tied to the temporal sequence, the absent s189(3) notice, the absent consultation and the comparator retention rather than asserted in the abstract.

what_needs_work: The unsupported 'safety context giving rise to the allegation' phrase in the first settlement term must be removed; it has no basis anywhere in the case brief and is a fabricated fact that materially damages factual fidelity and credibility.

The settlement compensation clause anchors to the 12-month section 194(1) ceiling despite the legal claims paragraph expressly invoking the higher 24-month section 194(3) ceiling for the pregnancy-linked AUD claim; this inconsistency undersells leverage in a HIGH-merit matter and should be resolved by aligning the settlement rationale with the AUD exposure actually pleaded.

The statutory entitlements legal claim paragraph substantially duplicates the settlement terms covering notice, leave pay and severance; tighten the claim paragraph to focus on the exposure/confirmation issue and let settlement terms carry the itemised mechanics.

The compensation proposal reads as a generic 'higher end of the range' statement rather than explicitly connecting the proposed settlement level to the specific procedural and substantive risk factors identified (no notice, no consultation, pregnancy timing, comparator), which the HIGH-merit check requires.
risks_to_monitor: If the 'safety context' fabrication reaches the Client or the counterparty in final form, it risks being read as referencing a wholly separate and unsubstantiated allegation, which could damage credibility and invite a sharp rebuttal from the Employer's representative.

The Employer may produce financial or restructuring records showing the two new clients did not affect headcount needs in the Client's specific team, which would weaken the substantive retrenchment argument; the letter should be calibrated to survive that counter-evidence.
